title: Why Does Beer Give Me a Headache? Causes and Fixes
excerpt: Why beer gives you a headache, even after one: alcohol strength, carbonation, histamine, tyramine, gluten, and the hops myth, plus how to stop it.
metaDescription: Why does beer give you a headache, even after one? Alcohol strength, histamine, tyramine, gluten, and the hops myth, plus how to prevent it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** if beer gives you a headache, the most likely cause is the alcohol itself, made worse by how beer is usually drunk: big pours, fast, on an empty stomach, and often at a higher strength than people realize. A 16 oz pint of a 7% IPA is close to two standard drinks, not one. For some people, things that are more common in beer than in clear spirits can add to the problem, including **histamine** and **tyramine** (natural compounds made during fermentation), and, for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity, the gluten from barley and wheat. Hops get a lot of the blame online, but there is no good evidence that hops themselves cause headaches. Most beer headaches can be prevented by choosing lower-strength beer, slowing down, and eating first.

This page is about the headache that comes on **while you're drinking or within a few hours afterward**, including the frustrating one that shows up after a single beer. That's a different thing from the pounding head you wake up with the next morning. If the morning after is your problem, our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) covers that side, and our broader [alcohol headache guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explains both kinds of headache for every type of drink.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research for education. It doesn't replace a doctor who knows your health history. **Get urgent medical care (call 911 in the US)** if a headache comes on suddenly and severely (the worst headache of your life, reaching full strength within about a minute), or if it comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, trouble seeing, or a seizure. Those aren't beer headaches. **See a doctor soon** if one beer reliably gives you a headache, if your headaches are getting more frequent, if beer brings on wheezing, hives, or swelling, or if you take a medicine that interacts with alcohol or tyramine, such as an MAOI antidepressant.

## Two Kinds of Beer Headache

Headache specialists recognize two separate headaches caused by alcohol, and it helps to know which one you're getting, because they have different causes and different fixes.

1. **The immediate headache.** This one starts while you're drinking or within about three hours of your first drink. It's sometimes called a "cocktail headache." It tends to be a throbbing pain on both sides of the head or across the forehead, and it often gets worse if you move around. It usually fades within a few hours of stopping drinking. This is the headache people mean when they say "one beer gives me a headache."
2. **The delayed headache.** This is the hangover headache. It shows up the next morning, often after blood alcohol has dropped to around zero, and it comes with the rest of the hangover package: tiredness, nausea, thirst, and feeling foggy.

The International Classification of Headache Disorders, the reference system doctors use to diagnose headaches, lists both. It also notes that people who already get migraines are more likely to get the immediate type, and that it can be triggered by much smaller amounts of alcohol in those people.

If your headache arrives during the second beer, it's the immediate kind, and the rest of this page is mostly about that. If it arrives at 7 a.m., the [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) is the better place to start.

## Why Does Beer Give Me a Headache? The Main Causes

There's no single "beer headache" chemical. Several things stack up, and different people react to different parts of the stack. Here they are roughly in order of how often they're likely to be the culprit.

### 1. Alcohol itself, and how fast it reaches your blood

Alcohol (ethanol) widens blood vessels, including those in and around the head, and it affects pain signaling in the brain. In people prone to headaches, that's enough on its own to start one. The faster your blood alcohol rises, the more likely this is. That's why the same two beers can feel fine at a long dinner and give you a headache at a standing-room bar.

Beer has a few features that make a fast rise easy:

- **Carbonation.** Fizzy drinks seem to empty from the stomach into the small intestine faster, and the small intestine is where most alcohol is absorbed. Research on carbonated mixers suggests bubbles can speed up how quickly alcohol reaches the blood for some people.
- **Volume.** Beer goes down easily, especially cold on a hot day. People often drink a pint in the time they'd sip half a glass of wine.
- **Empty stomach.** Beer is the classic "first drink after work" before dinner. Food in the stomach slows alcohol absorption a lot, so drinking on an empty stomach makes the rise steeper.

### 2. The beer is stronger than you think

This is the most underrated cause, especially among craft beer drinkers. A "standard drink" in the US is about 0.6 oz of pure alcohol, which equals a 12 oz can of 5% beer. But very few craft beers are served that way.

| What you're drinking | Roughly how many standard drinks |
|---|---|
| 12 oz light lager, 4.2% | about 0.85 |
| 12 oz regular lager, 5% | about 1 |
| 16 oz pint of lager, 5% | about 1.3 |
| 16 oz pint of IPA, 7% | about 1.9 |
| 16 oz can of double IPA, 8.5% | about 2.3 |
| 12 oz imperial stout, 10% | about 2 |

So "I only had two beers" can easily be four drinks' worth of alcohol, drunk in an hour. If you get headaches from IPAs but not from lagers, this alone may explain it, before hops even come into it. You can check the ABV on the can or menu and do the rough math: ounces multiplied by ABV, divided by 0.6.

### 3. Histamine

Histamine is a natural compound your body uses in allergic reactions and in regulating blood vessels. It's also made by bacteria and yeast during fermentation, so beer, wine, cheese, and other fermented foods contain some. Histamine widens blood vessels and can trigger headaches, flushing, a stuffy nose, and itchy skin in people who are sensitive to it.

Your gut normally breaks down histamine from food using an enzyme called diamine oxidase (DAO). Some people make less of it, a condition often called histamine intolerance, and alcohol may also interfere with how well DAO works. That's a double hit: you take in some histamine and you're less able to break it down.

How much histamine is in beer varies a lot by style and brewing method. As a general pattern, beers that go through extra bacterial fermentation (sours, some Belgian styles, and some unfiltered or barrel-aged beers) tend to carry more than clean, filtered lagers. Red wine is usually higher than most beer, which is part of why the [red wine headache](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) is more famous. If beer also gives you a stuffy nose, flushing, or itchy skin, histamine is worth suspecting. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) goes into the details.

### 4. Tyramine

Tyramine is another compound formed during fermentation and aging. It can raise blood pressure and is a well-known migraine trigger for some people, which is why it shows up on lists of foods to watch alongside aged cheese and cured meats.

Tyramine matters most for one group: people taking **MAOI antidepressants** (such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or isocarboxazid) or some other MAO-inhibiting drugs. Those medicines block the body's main way of breaking tyramine down, and a large tyramine load can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure, which can start with a sudden, severe headache. Dietary guidance for people on MAOIs has long singled out **tap or draft beer and home-brewed beer**, which can contain more tyramine than bottled or canned commercial beer. If you take one of these medicines, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking any beer, and treat a sudden severe headache after drinking as an emergency.

For everyone else, tyramine in typical commercial beer is a minor factor, but it may help explain why some migraine sufferers notice certain beers trigger them and others don't.

### 5. Gluten, for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity

Most beer is made from barley, and some from wheat. Both contain gluten. Headaches are a commonly reported symptom in people with celiac disease and in people with non-celiac gluten sensitivity. If you also get bloating, stomach pain, or diarrhea after beer but feel fine after wine or spirits, gluten is worth considering. Don't self-diagnose celiac disease by cutting out gluten first, though: the blood test is most accurate while you're still eating it, so talk to your doctor before you change your diet. Our [gluten-free alcohol guide](/never-hungover/gluten-free-alcohol) covers which drinks are naturally gluten-free and how "gluten-reduced" beer differs from gluten-free beer.

### 6. Congeners and other by-products

Congeners are the extra compounds that come along with alcohol during fermentation and aging: things like other alcohols, aldehydes, and esters that give drinks their flavor. They're linked mainly to worse hangovers rather than the immediate headache. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues (2010) found that people rated their hangovers as worse after bourbon, which is high in congeners, than after vodka, which is low, even at the same blood alcohol level. Beer sits somewhere in the middle. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains where different drinks fall.

### 7. Hops: the popular suspect

You'll read a lot of claims online that hops cause headaches, usually from people who get headaches from IPAs. There is no good evidence that hops cause headaches in ordinary drinkers. Hops contain many plant compounds, and a person could react to almost anything, but as a general explanation it doesn't hold up well. The simpler explanation for "IPAs give me a headache" is that IPAs are usually much stronger than lagers (see the table above) and are often served in 16 oz pours. If you want to test it, try a low-alcohol or non-alcoholic IPA. If the hoppy flavor is there and the headache isn't, it probably wasn't the hops.

### 8. Sulfites

Sulfites are best known from wine labels. Some beers contain small amounts, either formed naturally by yeast or added in processing. Sulfite sensitivity is real but uncommon, and it mainly shows up as breathing problems (wheezing, chest tightness), especially in people with asthma, rather than as headaches. Sulfites are an unlikely cause of most beer headaches. If you do get wheezing after beer, that's a reason to see a doctor, not just to switch brands.

### 9. Dehydration and blood sugar

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more than you drink. Beer is mostly water, which helps, and lower-strength beers are less dehydrating than strong ones. Even so, a long session of strong beer can still leave you behind on fluids. Dehydration contributes to headache, mostly the next morning. Drinking on an empty stomach can also cause your blood sugar to dip, which can add to headache and shakiness. Our page on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains the hydration side in more detail.

## Why Does Just One Beer Give Me a Headache?

A headache after a single beer, especially if it shows up within an hour, points away from "too much alcohol" and toward sensitivity. The most common explanations are:

- **You're migraine-prone.** People who get migraines are more likely to react to small amounts of alcohol. If your beer headache feels like your usual migraine (one-sided, throbbing, with light or sound sensitivity or nausea), alcohol is likely acting as a migraine trigger. Our [migraine after drinking guide](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) covers this in depth.
- **Histamine sensitivity.** A headache with flushing, a stuffy nose, or itchy skin after one beer suggests histamine.
- **An enzyme difference.** Some people, most commonly of East Asian descent, carry a variant of the ALDH2 gene that makes them slow to clear acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. They often flush bright red with a racing heart and a headache after a small amount of any alcohol, not just beer. This matters beyond the headache, because regular drinking with this variant is linked to a higher risk of esophageal cancer.
- **It wasn't really "one beer."** One 16 oz double IPA is more than two standard drinks.
- **Empty stomach plus carbonation.** One fizzy beer on an empty stomach after a long day can raise blood alcohol surprisingly fast.
- **Something other than the beer.** Skipped meals, poor sleep, stress, a stuffy bar, or caffeine withdrawal late in the day can all set up a headache that the beer simply tips over the edge.

Our guide to the [headache after one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) goes deeper into the single-drink headache for all types of alcohol.

## Why Does Beer Give Me a Headache but Not Liquor?

This is one of the most common versions of the question, and it's usually a mix of chemistry and habit.

**The chemistry side.** Clear spirits like vodka and gin are distilled, which strips out most of the histamine, tyramine, gluten proteins, and other fermentation by-products. Beer is not distilled, so all of those stay in. If you're sensitive to any of them, beer can trigger a headache that the same amount of alcohol from vodka would not. (Distilled spirits made from wheat or barley are generally considered gluten-free because distillation leaves the gluten behind, though some people with celiac disease still prefer to avoid them.)

**The habit side.** This part is easy to overlook. People tend to drink spirits and beer differently:

- A shot or a mixed drink usually contains one measured standard drink. A pint of craft beer may contain two.
- Spirits often come with a meal or are sipped slowly. Beer often comes first, fast, and before food.
- The amount of fluid in beer can make you feel like you're "drinking slowly" when you're actually taking in alcohol quickly.

**The honest test.** If you want to know whether it's really beer or just how you drink it, try matching the variables: same number of standard drinks, same pace, same food. If you still get a headache from the beer and not the spirit, something in the beer (histamine, tyramine, gluten, or something else) is probably the trigger for you. If the headache disappears once you match the pace and strength, the problem was the dose, not the drink.

Worth knowing: the old saying about the order you drink things in doesn't hold up. A 2019 study published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* found that drinking beer before wine, or wine before beer, made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. The total amount of alcohol mattered far more. Our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) page explains that research.

## Draft, Bottled, and Canned Beer

People sometimes notice that draft beer gives them a headache when the same beer in a bottle doesn't. A few possible reasons:

- **Pour size.** Draft is usually served in 16 oz pints or larger, compared with 12 oz bottles. That's a third more alcohol per glass.
- **Tyramine.** Unpasteurized draft beer can carry more tyramine than pasteurized bottled beer, which is why MAOI diet guides single it out.
- **Line cleanliness.** Poorly maintained tap lines can affect flavor, and there are anecdotal claims they cause headaches. There is no good evidence on that point, but a beer that tastes off is a reasonable thing to send back.
- **Setting.** Draft beer is often drunk at bars, standing up, in rounds, without food. That's the perfect setup for a fast rise in blood alcohol.

## Beer Styles: Which Are More Likely to Cause Headaches?

There's no beer that's guaranteed not to give you a headache, and individual sensitivity varies a lot. But some general patterns are reasonable to use as a starting point:

- **Lower risk:** light lagers, session beers (around 4% or less), and clean filtered pilsners. They have less alcohol per serving and tend to carry fewer fermentation by-products.
- **Higher alcohol risk:** IPAs, double IPAs, Belgian strong ales, barleywines, and imperial stouts. Many run 7% to 12%.
- **Possible histamine and tyramine risk:** sours and wild ales, some Belgian styles, aged or barrel-aged beers, and unfiltered or bottle-conditioned beers with live yeast.
- **Gluten-related:** standard barley and wheat beers. Gluten-free beers made from sorghum, rice, or millet are an option if gluten is your trigger.
- **Non-alcoholic beer:** if alcohol itself is the trigger, this is the most effective swap. Most "non-alcoholic" beers in the US can contain up to 0.5% alcohol, which is tiny for most people but still worth knowing. Our page on [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol) explains the labeling.

## How to Get Rid of a Beer Headache Fast

If you already have a headache from beer, here's what helps, in order:

1. **Stop drinking.** The immediate alcohol headache usually fades within a few hours once your blood alcohol starts to fall. Another beer will not "take the edge off."
2. **Drink water.** A large glass now and steady sips after. It won't cure the headache on its own, but it helps if dehydration is part of it.
3. **Eat something.** Food with some carbohydrate and protein helps steady blood sugar and slows absorption of any alcohol still in your stomach.
4. **Get somewhere quiet and dim.** Especially if the headache feels migrainous, light and noise make it worse.
5. **Cold or warm compress.** A cold pack on the forehead or back of the neck helps some people; others prefer warmth on tight neck muscles.
6. **Painkillers, carefully.** If you need one, choose with care:
   - **Ibuprofen or naproxen** are easier on the liver but can irritate the stomach, which alcohol already does. Take them with food and water. The labels warn people who have 3 or more drinks a day to ask a doctor first because of the risk of stomach bleeding. See our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).
   - **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is easier on the stomach but adds work for the liver. Don't take it while you're still drinking or "just in case" before bed. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the safe way to use it.
   - **Migraine medicines** such as triptans: if you already have a prescription, check with your doctor or pharmacist about using it after drinking.
7. **Sleep it off.** For most people the immediate beer headache is gone by morning. If it rolls straight into a hangover headache, see our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## How to Prevent a Beer Headache

The steps with the best support are simple and boring, and they work for most people:

- **Check the ABV and count standard drinks.** Swap a 7% IPA for a 4.5% lager and you cut the alcohol per pint by more than a third.
- **Order smaller pours.** A 10 oz or 12 oz glass instead of a pint is an easy, invisible change.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** A real meal before the first beer is one of the most effective things you can do.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour, and slow down further for strong beer.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between beers slows your pace and helps with fluids.
- **Try a non-alcoholic beer between rounds.** You keep the taste and the social ritual without the alcohol.
- **Keep a simple log.** Note the style, ABV, amount, whether you ate, and whether you got a headache. Within a few weeks most people can see their own pattern, whether it's a specific style, strength, or setting.
- **If you suspect histamine,** favor filtered, pasteurized lagers over sours and unfiltered styles, and talk to your doctor before trying antihistamines with alcohol. Some antihistamines cause drowsiness that alcohol makes much worse; our [antihistamines and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) covers which ones.
- **If you suspect gluten,** try a certified gluten-free beer or a different drink and see your doctor about testing.
- **If you get migraines,** talk to your doctor about whether alcohol is a trigger for you and whether to avoid it entirely.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

We're a site about dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, so it's fair to ask whether it helps with beer headaches. The honest answer is that **no study has tested DHM on beer headaches**, and there is no good evidence that it prevents them.

What's known about DHM comes mostly from animal and lab research, with limited human data. Some animal studies suggest it may support the enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde, which is why people use it to feel better the morning after a night out. That could be relevant to the delayed hangover headache. It does nothing for histamine, tyramine, gluten reactions, or migraine, and it won't make a 9% double IPA behave like a light lager.

If you already use DHM for hangovers, there's no reason to stop, and you can notice for yourself whether your beer nights feel different. Just don't count on it to fix a headache that hits after one beer. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people use it and what the research shows, and our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the strategies with the best evidence. If you want to try it, a plain single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Choosing a lower-strength beer and eating first will still do more for an immediate beer headache than any supplement.

## When to See a Doctor

> **When to see a doctor about beer headaches.** Most beer headaches are an annoyance, not a danger, and they go away once you stop drinking. But see a doctor if:
>
> - One beer, or even a few sips, reliably gives you a headache.
> - Your headaches are getting more frequent or more severe, or you're reaching for painkillers after most nights out.
> - Beer headaches feel like migraines, or alcohol seems to be triggering your migraines more often.
> - You get wheezing, chest tightness, hives, or swelling of the lips, tongue, or face after drinking. These suggest an allergic-type or sulfite reaction.
> - You get bloating, stomach pain, or diarrhea along with the headache, which could point to celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
> - You flush bright red with a racing heart after small amounts of alcohol.
> - You take an MAOI antidepressant or any medicine with an alcohol warning on the label.
>
> **Get emergency care right away** for a sudden, severe "worst ever" headache, a headache with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness, numbness, slurred speech, vision changes, or a seizure, or a sudden severe headache after drinking beer while taking an MAOI. Call 911 in the US.
>
> **A separate note for people who drink every day:** if you get headaches, shakiness, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you go without alcohol for a day or so, those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal rather than a beer headache. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so don't stop suddenly on your own. Talk to a doctor, who can help you cut back safely.

## The Bottom Line

Beer headaches are real, and most of them come down to the alcohol: strong beers in big pours, drunk quickly on an empty stomach, with carbonation speeding things up. For some people, beer also brings triggers that clear spirits don't, mainly histamine, tyramine, and gluten. Hops and sulfites are popular suspects, but there is no good evidence that they cause most beer headaches.

The fixes are practical: check the ABV, choose smaller and lighter pours, eat first, slow down, and alternate with water. Keep a short log to find your own trigger. And if one beer reliably gives you a headache, or headaches come with wheezing, swelling, gut symptoms, or a medicine warning, it's worth a conversation with your doctor. If you want to compare drinks more broadly, our guide to [which alcohol causes the least hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) ranks the common options.

## Frequently Asked Questions
**Why does beer give me a headache?**

Usually because of the alcohol itself. Alcohol widens blood vessels and affects pain signaling, and beer is often drunk quickly, on an empty stomach, in pints that can hold close to two standard drinks. Carbonation can also speed absorption. For some people, histamine, tyramine, or gluten in beer adds to the problem. There is no good evidence that hops cause headaches for most people.

**Why does one beer give me a headache?**

A headache after a single beer usually points to sensitivity rather than too much alcohol. Common reasons include being prone to migraines, sensitivity to histamine, an inherited difference in how you clear acetaldehyde (often with bright red flushing), drinking on an empty stomach, or a beer that is much stronger than a standard drink. If it happens reliably, it's worth mentioning to your doctor.

**Why does beer give me a headache but not liquor?**

Clear spirits are distilled, which removes most of the histamine, tyramine, gluten proteins, and fermentation by-products that stay in beer. Habits also differ: a mixed drink usually holds one measured drink, while a craft pint can hold two, and beer is often drunk faster and before food. Try matching the strength, pace, and food. If beer still gives you a headache, something in the beer is likely your trigger.

**Do hops cause headaches?**

There is no good evidence that hops cause headaches in most people. The usual reason IPAs seem to cause headaches is that they are stronger, often 6% to 9% alcohol, and served in 16 oz pours. To test it, try a non-alcoholic IPA. If you get the hoppy taste without the headache, the alcohol was more likely the cause.

**Can gluten in beer cause headaches?**

It can for people with celiac disease or non-celiac gluten sensitivity, where headaches are a commonly reported symptom. Bloating, stomach pain, or diarrhea after beer, but not after wine or spirits, makes gluten more likely. Talk to your doctor before cutting out gluten, because celiac testing is most accurate while you are still eating it.

**Which beer is least likely to give you a headache?**

Lower-strength, filtered, pasteurized beers such as light lagers and session beers are usually the safest bet, because they contain less alcohol per glass and fewer fermentation by-products. Strong IPAs, imperial stouts, sours, and unfiltered or barrel-aged beers are more likely to cause trouble. Non-alcoholic beer is the most reliable swap if alcohol is your trigger.

**How do I get rid of a beer headache fast?**

Stop drinking, have a large glass of water, eat something, and rest somewhere quiet and dim. If you need a painkiller, ibuprofen with food is often used but can irritate the stomach, and acetaminophen should not be taken while you are still drinking. The immediate beer headache usually fades within a few hours of stopping.

**Is a headache from beer an allergy?**

Usually not. True beer allergies are rare. A headache alone is far more likely to come from the alcohol, histamine, or migraine sensitivity. If you get hives, wheezing, chest tightness, or swelling of the lips, tongue, or face after beer, that suggests an allergic-type reaction, and you should see a doctor. Get emergency help for trouble breathing or throat swelling.

**Does DHM prevent beer headaches?**

No study has tested DHM on beer headaches, and there is no good evidence that it prevents them. DHM research is mostly from animal and lab studies on alcohol metabolism, which may be relevant to the next-morning hangover. It does nothing for histamine, tyramine, gluten, or migraine triggers. Lighter beer, smaller pours, and eating first will help more.
